title: Vale 1.0.0; prose linting for Drupal
description: Vale (for Drupal) holds every validated save to your style guide, from the node form or over JSON:API, and refuses the ones that break it. This post was written by AI and held to the same rules.

content.html: Drupal is 25 this year, and its code has had linters for a long time. Its words haven't, and with Drupal AI writing straight into the node form, more of them now come from a model. A search of drupal.org turns up readability scores and spellcheckers, but nothing that holds a save to your own style guide.

Vale (for Drupal) does that with the Vale prose linter. Break an error-level rule and the save is refused, or only the publish if drafts should save freely. 1.0.0 is out now for Drupal 10.3, 11 and 12, and needs the Vale binary on your server.

AI written, Vale linted, human reviewed. Claude wrote this post from the module's source, a test site where every command here was run, and notes from druxtjs.org. The "I" in it is me, Stuart, and I checked it before it went out.

Vale ran over every draft with this site's rules and caught 15 errors, from sentences stacked on the same opening to a stock "not this, but that" contrast. Simulated readers, one per audience, then reviewed it three times and caught what a linter can't: claims that didn't match the module. Each was fixed before you read it. Vale checks the sentence and ignores the author, so a model's prose meets the same rules as mine.

Vale in CI is the right tool for Markdown in a repository. Content in Drupal arrives through a save instead: the node form, a Fully Decoupled frontend over JSON:API, a workspace being published. The module checks there, on the server, whatever editor the author used.
drush vale:install puts the binary in bin/ beside your web root, checked against its published SHA-256:

content.title: Install the module and Vale, on a Composer site with Drush
content.code:
composer require drupal/vale
drush en vale
drush vale:install
content.highlighted: composer require drupal/vale drush en vale drush vale:install

content.html: Write a .vale.ini, run bin/vale sync beside it, deploy the styles directory with the site, and point settings.php at both:

content.title: settings.php
content.highlighted: $settings['vale_binary'] = $app_root . '/../bin/vale'; $settings['vale_config'] = $app_root . '/../.vale.ini'; // Optional. $config['vale.settings']['publish_only'] = TRUE; $config['vale.settings']['workspace_mode'] = 'block'; // Keyed by your Markdown text format's machine name. $config['vale.settings']['formats'] = ['markdown' => 'md'];

content.html: Then tick Check with Vale under Prose checks in a text field's settings, and the Status report confirms it.

Each field can set a minimum level, or change any rule's level or turn it off. With publish-only mode on, drafts save freely and the publish is held to the rules, following Content Moderation when it's installed.

content.alt: A Drupal edit form after a refused save. Two warnings ending "Blocks publishing" sit above an error that names the ai-tells HedgingPhrases and AICompoundPhrases rules, the line and the matched text.
content.caption: On druxtjs.org: a hedge and a cliché in a text paragraph, and the publish refused until they go.

content.html: Published styles are a start, but your own rules matter most: product names, words your organisation avoids, phrases your editors overuse. Each rule is a short YAML file in a folder under styles, kept in your codebase and deployed with the site:

content.title: styles/House/Terms.yml
content.code:
extends: substitution
message: "Use '%s' instead of '%s'."
level: error
ignorecase: false
swap:
  drupal: Drupal
  headless: Fully Decoupled
content.highlighted: extends: substitution message: "Use '%s' instead of '%s'." level: error ignorecase: false swap: drupal: Drupal headless: Fully Decoupled

content.html: Add House to BasedOnStyles in .vale.ini, and a save with "headless drupal" in it is refused. drush vale:check node.article.body "Some text." tries a rule against a field before an editor meets it. Levels are the site builder's call, so start a new rule at warning and promote it once you trust it.

Vale's styles documentation covers the other checks, from banned words to sentence length, and you can browse published styles in Vale's explorer. The rules this post was held to are in this site's .vale.ini.

This is the part I built it for. On a Fully Decoupled site, a Druxt or Nuxt frontend writes over JSON:API, and the check runs in the entity's validation, which those writes go through as well as the form. Post a body with a repeated word, with Vale's built-in style on, and you get a 422 that points at the field:

content.title: POST /jsonapi/node/article, with "Check the the docs." in the body
content.highlighted: { "errors": [ { "title": "Unprocessable Content", "status": "422", "detail": "body.0.value: Body: Vale.Repetition: 'the' is repeated! (line 1: \"the the\")", "source": { "pointer": "/data/attributes/body/value" } } ] }

content.html: Several errors in one value share that entry, one per line of detail, each naming its field. With publish-only mode on, a refused publish comes back on the entity, at /data, still naming the field. Warnings and suggestions come back in meta.vale, on a refused write or a successful one, with checked false if Vale couldn't run:

content.title: meta.vale on a 201, with a warning
content.highlighted: { "meta": { "vale": { "checked": true, "alerts": [ { "entity_type": "node", "bundle": "article", "id": "a22048fc-b0ec-4a9b-a80b-14be85498d81", "field": "body", "delta": 0, "rule": "Microsoft.Adverbs", "level": "warning", "message": "Remove 'very' if it's not important to the meaning of the statement.", "line": 1, "start": 9, "end": 12, "match": "very", "description": "", "link": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/word-choice/use-simple-words-concise-sentences" } ] } } }

content.html: So a Fully Decoupled editor gets the same feedback as the node form, without rebuilding the rules in JavaScript.
POST /vale/check returns the alerts a field would get, with the sentence around each, and saves nothing. It's built for an editor that checks as you type, in Druxt or anywhere else.

content.title: POST /vale/check
content.code:
{ "entity_type": "node", "bundle": "article", "field": "body", "format": "basic_html", "text": "

Check the the docs. This step is very easy to miss.

" }
content.highlighted: { "entity_type": "node", "bundle": "article", "field": "body", "format": "basic_html", "text": "<p>Check the the docs. This step is very easy to miss.</p>" }

content.title: The response
content.highlighted: { "checked": true, "publish_only": true, "alerts": [ { "rule": "Vale.Repetition", "level": "error", "message": "'the' is repeated!", "match": "the the", "sentence": "Check the the docs." }, { "rule": "Microsoft.Adverbs", "level": "warning", "message": "Remove 'very' if it's not important to the meaning of the statement.", "match": "very", "sentence": "This step is very easy to miss.", "link": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/word-choice/use-simple-words-concise-sentences" } ] }

content.html: A caller needs the Use the Vale check endpoint permission and edit access to the field, and a cookie session sends an X-CSRF-Token.

Before a workspace is published, the module checks everything in it. With workspace_mode set to block, the publish is refused while anything has an error or a value can't be checked, even though an ordinary save goes through when Vale can't run. The default, advise, publishes and lists the findings.

Publish-only mode and workspaces suit each other. Inside a workspace every save is a draft, including an edit to a page that's already live, so editors save freely and the workspace's publish is where the rules apply, in advise mode as well as block. drush vale:lint --workspace=stage runs the same check from a deploy script.

content.alt: Two Drupal messages after a refused workspace publish. The error lists a Vale.Repetition and a Microsoft.Contractions finding on the body of a node called Release notes, then a summary: Stage, 2 prose errors, 1 warning or suggestion. A warning below lists a Microsoft.Adverbs finding.
content.caption: Publishing the Stage workspace, refused: two errors in a draft, and the warning listed beside them.

content.html: Vale ships as one binary, and it has to be on every web server and in the CLI container. drush vale:install covers Linux and macOS. On a container host, build it into every image that serves Drupal or runs Drush, as druxtjs.org does on Lagoon, and add gcompat on Alpine. Other managed hosts are on the 1.1.0 list.

On a test site, Vale added about 55 ms to an uncached JSON:API save of a short paragraph, and nothing when the text hadn't changed, because results are cached until the text or the styles do. If Vale is missing or times out, the content saves and the author is told it wasn't checked, unless you set fail_closed.

For saves that skip validation, like a migration, drush vale:lint checks the content afterwards and exits with 1, so a deploy can depend on it. Any text field you opt in is checked, on a Drupal CMS site too. The title is a base field rather than one you opt in, and Canvas keeps its text in component props, so neither is checked.

content.description: The code is on GitHub, and the issue queue is on Drupal.org. If your editors rely on Vale, sponsoring is what funds the next release.

content.html: Next up are hooks for other modules and summary fields, with AI-suggested rewrites further out. What would you want it to do for your editors?
